pages.title: About
pages.content: This page is being written. Madoka Childcare was founded in 2015 by Madoka Quinlan at 12 Linden Row, Ranelagh, Dublin 6.

pages.title: The care day
pages.content: The day runs from 07:30 to 18:30, Monday to Friday. The full day, hour by hour, is set out here.

pages.title: Rooms & ages
pages.content: Nest takes babies from 4 to 15 months, Meadow from 15 to 30 months and Grove from 2½ to 4 years: 39 places in three rooms.

pages.title: Educators
pages.content: Every child has a key person. The people who work at the house are introduced here.

pages.title: Food & kitchen
pages.content: Meals are cooked in the house kitchen each morning. Meals, nappies, wipes and sun cream are included in the fee.

pages.title: Fees & hours
pages.content: Fees are in euro, paid in 12 monthly payments: five days €1,480, four days €1,240, three days €980, two days €690, an extra day €78 and a one-off registration of €150.

pages.title: Enrolment & settling in
pages.content: Visit, place offer, a family meeting with your key person, a two-week settling-in and a first full day.

pages.title: Families' stories
pages.content: Three families describe, in their own words, how the first weeks went.

pages.title: Questions
pages.content: What parents ask us first: sick days, naps, nappies, late pickup and settling in.

pages.title: Visit & contact
pages.content: Visits are on Tuesday and Thursday at 10:00 and 16:00. Call +353 1 555 0172 or write to hello@madoka-childcare.example.

posts.title: What we cook in a week
posts.excerpt: Tomás Rivera cooks lunch and an afternoon snack in the house kitchen every morning.
posts.content:
Tomás Rivera starts in the kitchen before the doors open at 07:30. Lunch is at 11:30 and the afternoon snack at 15:00, and both are cooked in the house, not brought in.

A week in the Meadow and Grove rooms runs from a vegetable stew on Monday to fish and potatoes on Friday, with fruit and a plain biscuit or toast for the snack. Babies in the Nest eat purées or soft finger food, depending on where they are.

If your child has an allergy or a dietary need, tell Hanna Kowalski at the visit so the kitchen knows from the first day.

posts.title: Why naps don't follow the clock
posts.excerpt: In the Nest, naps and feeds follow each baby; from 12:30 the older rooms rest together.
posts.content:
Babies do not sleep by the clock, so in the Nest we do not ask them to. Each baby has a cot, a blanket from home if you like, and a key person who knows the signs of tiredness.

From 12:30 Meadow and Grove rest together in the quiet room, with curtains half drawn and low cots. Some children sleep, some lie and look at the ceiling, and both are fine.

Tell your key person about a short night. It changes how the morning goes and how early we start the rest.

posts.title: Washing hands, forty times a day
posts.excerpt: A low sink, a stool and an educator at the child's side: how handwashing becomes a habit.
posts.content:
There is a low sink in every room, with a soap dispenser a toddler can press. Hands are washed after the garden, before lunch, after nappies and after painting.

An educator stands beside the child and sings or counts while the water runs. By two and a half, most children in Grove wash their hands on their own and remind the adults.

It is a small habit, repeated all day, and it is one of the things families tell us they see at home.
